items.title: Two Unconventional Hall Effects in the Kagome Magnet TmMn4Cr$_2$Sn$_6$
items.summary: We identify two Hall anomalies in the kagome magnet TmMn$_4$Cr$_2$Sn$_6$. We propose that the high-field anomaly reflects a discontinuous spin reorientation and differing sublattice contributions to Hall transport and magnetization. At low fields, Hall hysteresis persists despite negligible magnetic hysteresis, suggesting a chirality-related contribution, although its microscopic origin remains unresolved. These contrasting regimes show how magnetic transitions can mimic unconventional Hall signals and highlight the limits of magnetization-based Hall decomposition.
items.author: Mohamed El Gazzah, Fehmi Sami Yasin, Bishal Thapa et al.

items.title: Study Finds Gene Importance Does Not Predict Mutation Rates
items.summary: Recent claims suggest that mutation is not entirely random, with arguments proposing that essential genes or those needed for rapid adaptation are protected or given higher mutation rates based on factors like gene importance and strand location. To evaluate these theories, researchers analyzed mutation accumulation data for wild-type Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae using a multiple parameter-controlled approach. The analysis accounted for protein levels, essentiality, transcription rates, and replication strands. The results showed nearly uniformly unsupportive trends that varied between species and exhibited negligible effect sizes. Highly essential or abundant proteins did not display lower mutation rates, and strand differences were absent in E. coli and other prokaryotes. Ultimately, the findings indicate that gene importance does not predict mutation rates, supporting the traditional view of mutation as a random process.
items.author: Sofia Radrizzani, Laurence D. Hurst
items.original_title: The importance of genes does not predict their mutation rate
items.original_summary: by Sofia Radrizzani, Laurence D. Hurst The convention that mutation is a random process has been challenged by suggestions that selection has acted on between-gene variation in the mutation rate, with claims that more important genes are protected from mutation in part, in prokaryotes, by being on the leading strand, while those required for rapid adaptive evolution have higher mutation rates, in part by being on the lagging strand. The original selectionist claims have proven contentious with several replication failures. However, none of the replication attempts fully allow for covariates and many employ data from mismatch repair (MMR) knockout strains.

items.title: Mice Use Sound Statistics and Interneurons to Detect Targets in Noise
items.summary: Detecting specific sounds within natural background noise like rain or wind remains a major challenge. While humans can leverage the statistical predictability of such sound textures, the underlying neural mechanisms are poorly understood. Researchers trained mice to detect vocalizations embedded in sound textures with varying statistical predictability while monitoring and modulating neural activity in the auditory cortex. The experiments revealed that mice perform better and show improved neural encoding when given more time to sample sound statistics per trial, or when listening to textures with higher cross-frequency correlations. Additionally, optogenetic activation of parvalbumin-positive interneurons played a crucial role in temporal integration, yielding asymmetric effects on detection depending on acoustic context. The study demonstrates that mice successfully exploit stimulus statistics to isolate sounds in noise.
items.author: Artoghrul Alishbayli, Karol Przewrocki, Paul van Heumen et al.
items.original_title: Neural integration of acoustic statistics enables mice to detect acoustic targets in noise
items.original_summary: by Artoghrul Alishbayli, Karol Przewrocki, Paul van Heumen, Bernhard Englitz Sound detection amidst noise presents an important challenge in audition. Many naturally occurring sounds (rain, wind) can be described and predicted only statistically, so-called sound textures. Previous research has demonstrated the human ability to leverage this statistical predictability for sound recognition, but the neural mechanisms remain elusive. We trained mice to detect vocalizations embedded in sound textures with different statistical predictability, while recording and optogenetically modulating the neural activity in the auditory cortex. Mice showed improved performance and neural encoding if they could sample the statistics longer per trial. Textures with more exploitable structure, specifically higher cross-frequency correlations improved behavioral performance as well as neural representation of vocalizations.

items.title: Category Learning Drives Attentional Gain in the Auditory Cortex
items.summary: Humans and animals develop cognitive specializations to process complex signals, such as voices that convey words alongside cues about identity and internal state. Expert perception requires discovering regularities and flexibly weighting information as task demands shift. Researchers investigated whether this process involves attentional gain by employing auditory category learning tasks where participants categorized novel soundscapes by alien identity and size. Using functional MRI, the team observed whether participants prioritized frequency bands diagnostic for identity. Only participants who achieved expert-level identity categorization showed neural prioritization of the diagnostic frequency band. This neural selectivity mirrored patterns driven by explicit, sustained selective attention to pure tones. The findings indicate that learning complex categories can directly drive attentional gain toward the specific input dimensions that are most diagnostic for the task.
items.author: Sahil Luthra, Raha N. Razin, Adam T. Tierney et al.
items.original_title: Category learning drives cortical attentional gain to diagnostic dimensions of perceptual information
items.original_summary: by Sahil Luthra, Raha N. Razin, Adam T. Tierney, Lori L. Holt, Frederic Dick Humans and other animals develop remarkable perceptual and cognitive specializations for identifying, differentiating, and acting on classes of ecologically important signals. This expertise is flexible enough to support diverse perceptual judgments: a voice, for example, simultaneously conveys what a talker says, as well as myriad cues about her identity and state. Expert perception across complex signals thus involves discovering and learning regularities that best inform diverse perceptual judgments, as well as weighting this information flexibly as task demands change. Here, we test whether this process may involve attentional gain.

items.title: Kelp Species Adjust Reproduction Strategy Based on Environmental Cues
items.summary: Many organisms alternate between distinct life stages and can switch between sexual and asexual reproduction, though the mechanisms coordinating these choices remain unclear. Researchers explored the molecular basis of life stage identity and reproductive modes in the kelp Laminaria pallida by combining gene expression analyses, developmental experiments, and population-level approaches. The study shows that asexual reproduction in this kelp is linked to endoreduplication and reduced fitness, and while it is preserved in natural populations, it is rarely expressed. Crucially, the presence of potential mating partners actively reduces asexual development, demonstrating that the kelp adjusts its reproductive mode depending on available opportunities. This conditional strategy allows asexual reproduction to serve as a backup when mates are scarce, while preserving the long-term benefits of sexual reproduction when partners are accessible.
items.author: Daniel Liesner, Rémy Luthringer, Lineekela Kandjengo et al.
items.original_title: Life-cycle plasticity enables conditional asexual reproduction in a kelp
items.original_summary: by Daniel Liesner, Rémy Luthringer, Lineekela Kandjengo, John J. Bolton, Mark D. Rothman, Myriam Valero, Fabian B. Haas, Susana M. Coelho Many organisms alternate between distinct life stages and can reproduce either sexually or asexually, yet the mechanisms coordinating these developmental and reproductive transitions remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the molecular basis of life stage identity and reproductive mode in the kelp Laminaria pallida , a multicellular organism with a complex life cycle. By combining gene expression analyses with developmental experiments and natural population-level approaches, we characterize the transcriptional signatures associated with developmental state transitions in both sexual and asexual contexts.

items.title: Decomposing Bacterial Pangenomes into Additive Gene Modules
items.summary: Bacterial pangenomes combine vertically inherited chromosomes with horizontally acquired mobile elements, creating complex architectures that traditional phylogenetic methods struggle to resolve. To address this, researchers utilized non-negative matrix factorization to decompose the accessory pangenome of 1,398 Staphylococcus aureus genomes into 24 additive gene modules called phylons. This framework cleanly separates lineage-defining components from mobile genetic elements with high accuracy and precision. The additive representation successfully recovered known biological structures and uncovered new insights, such as horizontal transfer events linking pandemic lineages. The approach also accurately discriminated host origins and antibiotic resistance profiles without retraining, while external validations on independent assemblies demonstrated robust performance. This organism-agnostic framework offers a scalable way to dissect the modular architecture of bacterial pangenomes.
items.author: Siddharth M. Chauhan, Bernhard O. Palsson, Jonathan M. Monk
items.original_title: Decomposition of the S. aureus pangenome reveals evolving genetic repertoire associated with adaptation and virulence
items.original_summary: by Siddharth M. Chauhan, Bernhard O. Palsson, Jonathan M. Monk Bacterial pangenomes are mosaics of vertically inherited chromosomal backgrounds and horizontally acquired mobile elements, yet existing analysis methods either assign each genome to a single phylogenetic group or treat genes independently, failing to resolve this composite architecture. Here, we show that non-negative matrix factorization decomposes the accessory pangenome of 1,398 curated Staphylococcus aureus genomes into 24 additive gene modules (“phylons”) that cleanly separate lineage-defining components from mobile genetic element repertoires, achieving 90% reconstruction accuracy with 96% precision. The additive representation, where each genome equals a primary lineage phylon plus one or more mobilome phylons, recovers known biology (clonal complex structure, immune evasion cluster types) and reveals previously uncharacterized structure, including multiple horizontal transfer events linking the CC30 and hybrid ST239 pandemic lineages.

items.title: Updated GapMind Tool Enhances Prokaryotic Amino Acid Pathway Analysis
items.summary: Researchers have updated the automated web-based tool GapMind to better annotate amino acid biosynthesis pathways in archaeal and bacterial genomes. By combining comparative genomics and high-throughput genetics, the team identified candidate genes to fill previously unknown metabolic gaps and verified the activity of ten new enzymes using cross-species complementation assays. Notable additions include a new route to glycine via glyoxylate, alternative enzymes for phosphoserine phosphatase, N-succinyl-L,L-diaminopimelate desuccinylase, N-acetylornithine deacetylase, and a putative bifunctional MetB/MetC. Following these updates, the average number of unexplained missing steps in amino acid biosynthesis across 208 high-quality prokaryotic genomes dropped significantly from 1.4 to 0.7 per genome. The remaining gaps are predominantly tied to the gain or loss of phosphate groups.
items.author: Morgan N. Price, Valentine V. Trotter, Markus de Raad et al.
items.original_title: Novel enzymes for amino acid biosynthesis in diverse bacteria and archaea: GapMind 2026
items.original_summary: by Morgan N. Price, Valentine V. Trotter, Markus de Raad, Suzanne M. Kosina, Hira P. Lesea, Anthony L. Shiver, Leslie A. Day, Surya Tripathi, Marta Torres, Trenton K. Owens, Audrey Liwen Wang, Anna Lisa Fear, Xuanyu Tao, Jizhong Zhou, Adam M. Deutschbauer, Adam P. Arkin We previously described GapMind, an automated web-based tool for annotating amino acid biosynthesis pathways in bacterial and archaeal genomes. We used GapMind to identify gaps in biosynthetic pathways and systematically used comparative genomics and high-throughput genetics to identify candidate genes to fill these gaps. We confirmed the activity of ten of the proposed enzymes by using cross-species complementation assays.
items.ai_title: Updated GapMind Tool Enhances Prokaryotic Amino Acid Pathway Analysis
items.ai_summary: Researchers have updated the automated web-based tool GapMind to better annotate amino acid biosynthesis pathways in archaeal and bacterial genomes. By combining comparative genomics and high-throughput genetics, the team identified candidate genes to fill previously unknown metabolic gaps and verified the activity of ten new enzymes using cross-species complementation assays. Notable additions include a new route to glycine via glyoxylate, alternative enzymes for phosphoserine phosphatase, N-succinyl-L,L-diaminopimelate desuccinylase, N-acetylornithine deacetylase, and a putative bifunctional MetB/MetC. Following these updates, the average number of unexplained missing steps in amino acid biosynthesis across 208 high-quality prokaryotic genomes dropped significantly from 1.4 to 0.7 per genome. The remaining gaps are predominantly tied to the gain or loss of phosphate groups.

items.title: Fish Virus Protein Exploits FTR86 to Inhibit Innate Immunity
items.summary: Researchers explored the role of the fish-specific TRIM subfamily protein EcFTR86 during Singapore grouper iridovirus infection. They found that EcFTR86 localizes to lysosomes and is heavily upregulated in grouper spleen cells during viral infection. Overexpressing EcFTR86 promoted viral replication, while knocking it down reduced infection, confirming its role as a pro-viral factor. Mechanistically, EcFTR86 negatively regulated type I interferon signaling by triggering the autophagic degradation of the STING-TBK1 axis, a process mediated by the cargo receptor Tollip. Furthermore, the viral protein VP018 interacted with EcFTR86 to accelerate this targeted degradation and suppress the host interferon response.
items.author: Linyong Zhi, Mengdi Yuan, Guimei Zhang et al.
items.original_title: Singapore grouper iridovirus VP018 exploits FTR86 to promote viral replication through Tollip-mediated degradation of the STING-TBK1 axis
items.original_summary: by Linyong Zhi, Mengdi Yuan, Guimei Zhang, Dongmiao Xiao, Xinyi Ren, Qiwei Qin, Xiaohong Huang, Youhua Huang Members of the tripartite motif (TRIM) family have been demonstrated to exert crucial roles in immune defense against pathogens. However, functions of the fish-specific TRIM subfamily (FTR), which lacks mammalian orthologues, remains poorly understood. In the current study, we investigated the potential roles of grouper FTR86 (EcFTR86) on innate immune response and its actions during fish virus infection. EcFTR86 was found to localize to lysosomes, and its transcription was significantly up-regulated in grouper spleen cells upon Singapore grouper iridovirus (SGIV) infection. Notably, the exogenous expression of EcFTR86 markedly enhanced SGIV replication, whereas knockdown of endogenous EcFTR86 significantly attenuated viral infection, demonstrating that EcFTR86 functions as a pro-viral factor against virus infection.

items.title: Study Links Social Media Integration to PTSD Symptoms Among South African Students
items.summary: A cross-sectional study of 491 South African university students investigated how social media integration relates to PTSD-consistent symptomatology, with a focus on problem-solving appraisals and perceived social support. The findings indicate that higher social media integration correlates positively with increased PTSD symptom severity across multiple clusters. Conversely, effective problem-solving appraisals and perceived social support appear to act as protective factors. Problem-solving partially mediated the link between social media use and symptom severity, while social support moderated several specific symptom dimensions. Researchers suggest that interventions bolstering coping strategies and social networks could help mitigate trauma-related distress among frequent social media users.
items.author: Tyrone B. Pretorius, Anita Padmanabhanunni
items.original_title: Problem-solving and social support appraisals in the cross-sectional association between social media integration and PCL-5 symptom severity
items.original_summary: by Tyrone B. Pretorius, Anita Padmanabhanunni The present study investigated the relationship between social media integration and PTSD-consistent symptomatology among South African university students, with a specific focus on the roles of problem-solving appraisal and perceived social support. Participants were 491 students who completed the Social Media Use Integration Scale, the Problem-Solving Inventory-20, the Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support, and the Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, correlations, and mediation and moderation analyses with PROCESS. Social media integration was positively associated with overall PTSD-consistent symptomatology and all symptom clusters measured by the PCL-5.

items.title: Study Examines Myeloid Transcriptional Programs and Ex Vivo Sensitivity in ARDS
items.summary: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is biologically diverse, prompting researchers to investigate how myeloid transcriptional programs relate across blood and lung compartments. The study evaluated whether a pre-specified neutrophil degranulation program and a perturbation-response module provide convergent evidence across public cohorts. Utilizing patient samples, purified neutrophil comparisons, and ex vivo treatments, researchers assessed gene coexpression networks and cellular responses. Results showed that the neutrophil degranulation program increased consistently in ARDS patients, rose after granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor exposure, and decreased following broad PI3K inhibition. However, the findings support an ARDS-associated myeloid effector program rather than establishing a prognostic signature, a causal outcome mechanism, or targeted therapeutic efficacy.
items.author: Wei Wei, Jing Liu, Ying Zhou et al.
items.original_title: Paired neutrophil association and ex vivo perturbation sensitivity define a bounded myeloid activation model in ARDS
items.original_summary: by Wei Wei, Jing Liu, Ying Zhou, Rui Zhao, LinGang Zhang Background Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is biologically heterogeneous, but how myeloid transcriptional programmes relate across blood and lung compartments remains uncertain. We examined whether a pre-specified neutrophil effector/degranulation programme and a separately derived perturbation-response module provide convergent, boundary-aware evidence across public cohorts. Methods Patient-level analyses descriptively localized programmes in a seven-patient peripheral blood mononuclear cell cohort and assessed paired bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and longitudinal alveolar-macrophage profiles. PBMC disease groups were severely confounded with expression-inferred sex. In purified neutrophils, paired ARDS–healthy-volunteer comparisons and healthy-donor granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF)/broad phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) perturbations were analysed separately.

items.title: Study Links Social Media Dietary Habits and Behavioral Constructs in University Students
items.summary: University students frequently encounter nutrition information, peer norms, and food marketing on digital platforms, yet research connecting these exposures to Integrated Behavioral Model constructs remains limited. A cross-sectional study of 385 undergraduates at King Khalid University investigated these dynamics using an Arabic questionnaire on social media and dietary habits. The findings revealed that all model constructs were positively correlated with dietary habits. Multiple linear regression indicated that positive attitudes, regular physical activity, and moderate daily social media use of up to four hours were associated with higher dietary habit scores. These results highlight that behavioral beliefs and lifestyle contexts can inform digital nutrition programs aimed at young adults.
items.author: Amani Alhazmi, Maha Ali, Manal Mohammed Hawash et al.
items.original_title: Social media–related dietary behaviors and integrated behavioral model constructs among university students: A cross-sectional study
items.original_summary: by Amani Alhazmi, Maha Ali, Manal Mohammed Hawash, Bali Sharma, Ali Mohieldin, Mahmoud Abdelwahab Khedr Background Social media exposes young adults to nutrition information, food marketing, peer norms, and health-related content. However, evidence on social media–related dietary behaviors and their links to Integrated Behavioral Model (IBM) constructs among Saudi university students is limited. This study examined these behaviors, IBM constructs, and factors associated with the Dietary Habits score among King Khalid University (KKU) students. Methods A cross-sectional study included 385 KKU undergraduates, recruited through convenience sampling between February and April 2026. Participants completed the Arabic IBM-based Social Media and Dietary Habits Questionnaire.

items.title: Researchers Find Evidence of Cretaceous Strandline Deposit in Wyoming's Lance Formation
items.summary: Excavations at the Hanson Ranch within the Maastrichtian Lance Formation of Wyoming have historically uncovered tens of thousands of disarticulated vertebrate fossils across various bonebeds. Recently, however, seven newly discovered quarries yielded associated remains of multiple dinosaur taxa, including Triceratops, Edmontosaurus, Thescelosaurus, and Anzu, in a configuration previously unseen at the site. These quarries align along a southeasterly direction, matching the orientation of long axes in many elongate bones found within the deposits. The preservation of associated skeletal elements indicates that soft-tissue connections or integumentary containment remained intact during transport and burial. Scientists conclude that these encapsulated, floating carcasses were stranded along a shoreline of the Western Interior Seaway.
items.author: Keith Snyder, Nelson Llempen, Caleb Darling et al.
items.original_title: Evidence for an upper cretaceous strandline deposit in the Lance Formation, Wyoming, USA
items.original_summary: by Keith Snyder, Nelson Llempen, Caleb Darling, Alessandro Franchini, Matthew McLain, Arthur Chadwick A series of apparently related quarries in the Maastrichtian (uppermost Cretaceous) Lance Formation of Wyoming provided the opportunity to evaluate the taphonomic mode for a suite of vertebrate fossils. Extensive work on the Hanson Ranch over the past three decades has exposed tens of thousands of fossils from dinosaur-bearing bonebeds. All of these bonebeds consist of disarticulated and disassociated remains. However, seven recently discovered quarries have yielded the remains of one or more dinosaur taxa (e.g., Triceratops, Edmontosaurus, Thescelosaurus, Anzu) in a state of association that was hitherto unknown on the ranch.

items.title: Systematic Evaluation of Training Data Generation Strategies for Machine Learning-Based Molecular and Materials Property Prediction
items.summary: Machine-learning (ML) models for molecular and materials property prediction are often trained on large datasets curated through arbitrary or generic sampling strategies. Such approaches can lead to the over- or under-representation of regions of chemical and materials space that are most relevant to the prediction task. An important challenge is therefore how to efficiently curate training data to maximize predictive performance while minimising the number of labelled examples required. Here, we systematically compare training data acquisition strategies for molecular and materials property prediction, ranging from random sampling to various active learning approaches. We evaluate their performance across different model classes, representations, datasets, and target properties.

items.title: Hubble Gravitational Lenses Prepare Ground for Roman Space Telescope
items.summary: A new gallery of gravitational lenses captured by the Hubble Space Telescope highlights diverse cosmic formations that will serve as targets for the upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Gravitational lensing happens when a massive foreground object bends and magnifies the light of a distant background object. Researchers use these distorted light patterns to study mass distribution and dark matter. While Hubble excels at high-resolution images of individual lenses, Roman will capture broader cosmic panoramas. Combining data from both observatories allows scientists to build precise lens models, detect small dark matter clumps, and improve understanding of galaxy evolution.

items.title: Large Pockels Effect in Multiaxial Ferroelectrics Induced by Polarization Reorientation
items.summary: Materials with large linear electro-optic (Pockels) effect have significant potential for fabricating energy-efficient photonic devices. Previous strategies have mostly relied on structural softness---associated with phase boundary, domain wall, or strain induced phase transition---to create large Pockels effect in ferroelectrics. In this Letter, we show that polarization reorientation in multiaxial ferroelectrics may create structural softness and thus induce large Pockels effect. By developing a phenomenological theory, we find that multiaxial ferroelectrics exhibit a hysteretic relationship between the azimuth angles of the polarization and the electric field, and a possible divergence of the linear electro-optic coefficient may occur at an appropriate polarization azimuth angle.

items.summary: As the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center at the California Science Center prepares to open an exhibit displaying the space shuttle Endeavour upright in launch position, NASA photographers are looking back at its final ferry flight on September 21, 2012. Millions watched as the shuttle flew atop a 747 carrier aircraft over major California landmarks. NASA team members engaged in extensive planning with local agencies, police departments, and aviation authorities to design a safe and scenic flight path. Photographers and videographers flew in escort fighter jets and police helicopters to document the historic journey, capturing iconic images of the spacecraft's farewell tour across the state.

items.title: Discrete anomaly inflow from SymTFT of $U(1)$ global symmetry: the modified Villain resolution
items.summary: We construct a lattice SymTFT for a $U(1)$ global symmetry with anomaly coefficient $k$ using the modified Villain formulation, in which the spin structure required for odd $k$ is realised explicitly by lattice Majorana fermions. We demonstrate that the same Majorana fermions sit at the junctions of the symmetry lines, exactly where the fusion of two $U(1)$ elements wraps around the circle. From the lattice algebra of lines and junctions we derive the $R$- and $F$-symbols in the bulk and on the gapped boundary, and show that for odd $k$ the boundary $F$-symbol obeys the Gu-Wen relation for the $U(1)$ symmetry defect, without passing through a bosonic shadow.

items.title: Is Spin Slow in Hot QCD?
items.summary: Promoting spin to a hydrodynamic variable requires slow relaxation, as mass-suppressed helicity flips in hot QCD suggest. Using the full leading-order collision operator, we show instead that light-quark spin damps at the transport rate $g^4T\ln(1/g)$, nearly as fast as vector currents. Since spatial spin locks to momentum, helicity-conserving soft, small-angle scatterings readily rotate it. Damping involves multiple kinetic modes beyond a single relaxation time, global rotation adds only reversible precession, and stronger coupling further disfavors a slow spin mode in quark-gluon plasma.

items.title: Accelerating solitons in Rindler space
items.summary: Relativistic nonlinear field theories that are integrable in two-dimensional Minkowski spacetime remain integrable in Rindler space. We investigate the properties of classical sine-Gordon (SG) solitons in Rindler space. Accelerating observers in each of the two Rindler wedges can see only a portion of the full soliton in Minkowski spacetime; this portion itself forms a soliton carrying a partial topological charge. The soliton solution admits the following interpretation: a soliton incoming from the horizon decelerates to stop at some point, then falls back and accelerates to the speed of light toward the horizon. Energy can flow into and out of the Rindler horizon.
items.author: Huiquan Li, Jianyong Wang

items.title: Matching lattice and continuum chiral determinants at finite volume
items.summary: Recent formulations of lattice chiral gauge theories define a complex fermion weight either through Craig's gauge-invariant overlap measure or, following Hsu and Witten, through a continuum Weyl determinant on a reconstructed gauge connection, with its phase fixed by the five-dimensional $η$-invariant. For one $SU(5)$ generation on a flat four-torus, we prove that their relative weights agree in the continuum limit along smooth gapped paths, after fixing a normalization and subtracting a local Yang-Mills counterterm, whose coefficient we determine. On bounded smooth families a uniform Dirac gap suffices: the vacuum expansion need not converge. We obtain explicit uniform convergence rates for the logarithmic variations and, for Craig's interpolation, prove the reconstruction bounds that the matching requires, extending Hsu's small-field comparison to finite amplitude.

items.title: Affine Vertex Operator Algebras and Correlation Functions on Elliptic Curves
items.summary: Let $V^{\Bbbk}(\mathfrak{g})$ be the universal affine vertex algebra attached to a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra at arbitrary level, and let $M=\bigoplus_{N=0}^{\infty}M_N$ be a $V^{\Bbbk}(\mathfrak{g})$ -module. We give an explicit formula for every genus-one trace of affine currents as a finite sum over cycle partitions. We then show the convergence of all fixed zero-mode trace series, hence absolute locally uniform convergence of the current traces and their meromorphic continuation on the elliptic configuration space. The same conclusion is obtained for arbitrary affine-state insertions. Finally, we compute the cases of at most four currents and the nodal limit $q\to 0$, in which the type-1 and type-2 elliptic cycle coefficients degenerate to rational genus-zero cycle coefficients and the module trace reduces to the ground-state space.

items.title: Poles Are Not Enough: Zeros of Dyson-Schwinger Gluon Propagators in Yang-Mills Thermodynamics
items.summary: A normalized two-point function with several poles does not, on its own, fix the source-free thermal partition function. For the Gaussian measure of the original gluon field, a positive-residue rational propagator contributes determinants from its poles and from zeros interlaced between them. The zero factors distinguish this completion from a gas of independent pole fields and restore two ultraviolet polarizations per adjoint eigenvalue at every finite truncation. We apply the construction to a background-covariant completion of the elliptic Dyson-Schwinger gluon kernel. The first-order SU(3) transition is already present with a single pole, and the saturated six-pole result shifts $T_c/M_g$ by only $1.48\%$, where $T_c$ is the coexistence temperature and $M_g$ is the lowest pole mass.
items.author: Marco Frasca, Anish Ghoshal, Stefan Groote

items.title: Thermodynamics within and across AdS Gauss--Bonnet holographic CFTs
items.summary: We study thermal competition within individual holographic conformal field theories (CFTs) and across theories with different anomaly coefficients in five-dimensional AdS Gauss--Bonnet gravity. We derive the work term conjugate to the dimensionless coupling from the boundary first law and use a common boundary clock to compare charged spherical saddles at fixed external source. Varying this source drives a first-order switch between the CFTs at the endpoints of the chosen coupling interval. In the unit-lapse cylinder clock with the zero-type-D vacuum energy, strict concavity at fixed radius reduces the global comparison to these two endpoints. The preferred coupling jumps across the coexistence line, whose slope is related to the entropy difference by a generalized Clapeyron relation.
items.author: Limin Zeng

items.title: Generalized Kosmann derivative and symmetry operators on Dirac structures
items.summary: We develop a spinorial symmetry framework for metric Dirac structures in $H$-twisted exact Courant algebroids. A generalized metric equips a Dirac structure with an intrinsic Riemannian Lie-algebroid geometry and identifies it isometrically with the positive subbundle of the generalized tangent bundle. For sections preserving the generalized metric, we prove an exact intertwining between the positive-spinor Kosmann--Dorfman action and the intrinsic Kosmann derivative. The comparison is independent of the auxiliary compatible generalized connection. Within the intrinsic geometry we derive Killing--Yano (KY) and conformal Killing--Yano (CKY) integrability identities, construct Killing-spinor-preserving operators from odd special KY and even special closed CKY forms, and obtain these forms from Hermitian bilinears of Killing spinors with imaginary Killing number.

items.title: Celestial Conjunction Captures Moon, Venus, and Spica Over Poland
items.summary: Planets shift relative to fixed stars in celestial movements known as conjunctions, which follow precise laws of celestial mechanics. An astronomical photo captured in Poland features a crescent Moon above the Tatra Mountains alongside bright Venus. Positioned near Venus is the bright star Spica, located in the constellation of Virgo. Spica, sitting about 250 light-years away, was historically identified as a binary star system containing two massive blue stars orbiting each other every four days. However, recent findings revealed that Spica functions as a triple star system.

items.title: Scotland's Flow Country Peat Bogs Store Vast Amounts of Carbon
items.summary: The Flow Country in northern Scotland features extensive blanket bogs that store massive amounts of carbon. Because these soggy, waterlogged soils prevent microbes from fully breaking down dead plant material, partially decayed matter accumulates into thick layers of peat. These unique ecosystems require abundant rainfall, poor drainage, and low evapotranspiration. Covering about 1,900 square kilometers of the Scottish Highlands, the area represents Europe's largest blanket bog ecosystem and the first of its kind to earn UNESCO World Heritage status. While forests typically store carbon in living trees that can release it when damaged, peat bogs can preserve carbon for thousands of years. Globally, peatlands cover a tiny fraction of Earth's land surface yet store more than twice as much carbon as all the world's forests combined.

items.title: Bright and Uniform Silicon Carbide Nanophotonic Arrays for Scalable Nanoscale Quantum Sensing
items.summary: Silicon carbide (SiC) spin defects are emerging as powerful platforms for nanoscale quantum sensing due to their near-surface stability, near-infrared emission, and CMOS compatibility. However, poor photon collection efficiency and the reliance on randomly distributed defects hinder the realization of practical, large-scale devices. Here, we demonstrate scalable, ultra-bright, and highly uniform SiC quantum nanophotonic arrays. By combining a self-aligned fabrication process with localized oxygen ion implantation, we deterministically position PL5 and PL6 centers at the exact center of 4H-SiC nanopillars. This architecture yields record-high photon count rates of $\sim$1 Mcps (PL5) and $\sim$2 Mcps (PL6), establishing a new benchmark for SiC color centers while maintaining near-identical brightness across the array.

items.title: Curiosity Completes Drilling at Nazca Site to Investigate Crystal Forms
items.summary: The Curiosity rover finished its drilling operations at the "Nazca" bedrock location, which features unique disk-shaped and potato chip-shaped crystal forms. Throughout the week, the rover delivered drill samples to the SAM instrument, conducted ChemCam LIBS measurements on various crystal targets like "Ahi Veremos," "Colca," and "Bermejo," and captured extensive Mastcam and RMI image mosaics. Environmental monitoring included dust devil surveys and horizon movies. Friday's plans prioritized imaging a solar eclipse by the Martian moon Phobos, executing nighttime MAHLI LED imaging of the crystals, and driving the rover away from the drill site to resume its southerly exploration route.

items.title: Integrated optical isolators enabled by 2D semiconductors via spin-momentum locking
items.summary: Integrated optical isolators based on spin-momentum locking hold great potential for protecting photonic integrated circuits from unwanted reflections. Currently, the most common implementations are magneto-optical isolators that require an externally applied magnetic field. Nevertheless, a wide range of nonreciprocal effects remains to be exploited in alternative material platforms. Although the majority of these effects induce changes to the propagation of light as a function of its polarization, they can be directly connected to the propagation direction through spin-momentum locking. We employ a computational approach to investigate various designs of integrated isolators based on nonreciprocal 2D semiconductors, studying the influence of their geometry and optical properties on the device performance.

items.title: Metasurfaces with Anisotropic Electric and Magnetic Conductivities: Parameter Retrieval for Arbitrary Incidence and Polarization
items.summary: Metasurfaces come in a great variety of unit cell geometries and material composition. A common approach for describing them relies on retrieving effective surface parameters (e.g., electric and magnetic conductivities) from plane-wave scattering data. Conventional retrieval methods are often limited to isotropic unit cells, a uniform host material, or lead to increased complexity by requiring reflection and transmission coefficients from both sides of the metasurface. Here, we derive analytical expressions for the equivalent surface conductivities of an electrically- and magnetically-polarizable anisotropic metasurface under oblique plane-wave incidence with arbitrary polarization. The proposed formulation does not require bidirectional scattering information, thus simplifying the process especially in experimental studies.
items.author: Dimitrios Chatzidimitriou, Alexandros Pitilakis, Odysseas Tsilipakos

items.title: Subwavelength registration of skull-compensating acoustic holograms via nonlinear parametric array feedback
items.summary: Realizing the potential of optimized acoustic holograms for applications like transcranial ultrasound requires sub-wavelength alignment accuracy (less than 1.5 mm at 1 MHz), which is difficult to achieve with current non-MRI optical neuro-navigation methods. To address the critical challenge of alignment, we leverage the parametric array (PA) signal as an alignment surrogate, a highly penetrative, low-frequency difference wave generated by the nonlinear mixing of two primary high-frequency beams. Simulations show that a misaligned skull-compensating lens increases the primary acoustic energy within the skull bone (volumetric energy trapping), which strengthens the nonlinear source of the PA signal. We also tested whether shear-mode conversion in bone contributes: 2D elastic simulations showed only a small (3-5%) increase in shear-type motion with misalignment, and the transmitted ex vivo bursts did not lengthen as a shear path would require.
items.author: Pradosh Pritam Dash, Costas D. Arvanitis

items.title: Learning a calibrated decision head from logged bandit feedback
items.summary: A decision head reads a state and a list of options and returns a probability per option in one forward pass. Once deployed, it usually observes only whether the option it chose was right: logged bandit feedback. We adapt such a head, LoRA on Qwen3-0.6B-Base and 1.7B-Base, from that feedback and report three results. First, the Brier or log score of the sampled action's own probability is not a usable REINFORCE reward: every wrong action earns at least gold's reward, with a mean baseline the lowest-probability wrong action gets the largest advantage, and at two options the signal is zero; in one run it cut accuracy on ordered-scale questions from .636 to .111.
items.author: Ye Yuan

items.title: TraceKV: Policy-Preserving Low-Rank KV Cache Compression for Reasoning Vision-Language Models
items.summary: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) impose substantial KV cache demands from both large multimodal contexts and growing reasoning traces. Low-rank KV compression has emerged as a promising paradigm that stores low-dimensional latents of KV states and can be combined with quantization. However, existing low-rank methods often induce growing predictive policy drift from the dense model when compressing reasoning KV states, resulting in reasoning failures. We identify two key causes of this degradation: calibration-state mismatch between static contexts and on-policy reasoning states, and unequal error sensitivity across KV states. To address these challenges, we propose TraceKV, a training-free low-rank KV compression framework that unifies on-policy calibration, sensitivity-aware SVD, and global rank allocation under a single policy-preserving principle, substantially reducing policy-KL divergence during reasoning.
items.author: Ke Li, Zishan Shao, Yiran Chen

items.title: Observations Drift, Structures Remain: Structural Pretraining with Time Alignment for Electromagnetic Signals
items.summary: Electromagnetic signal modeling is increasingly moving toward self-supervised pretraining on heterogeneous I/Q observations. However, an observed waveform is jointly shaped by signal generation, propagation environments, and acquisition processes, which mix reusable structural regularities with observation-specific variations. Existing methods usually pursue unified pretraining with reconstruction objectives on mixed observations. This heterogeneity creates two key mismatches for reconstruction pretraining: (1) appearance mismatch, induced by propagation-dependent waveform variations; and (2) temporal mismatch, induced by acquisition-dependent sampling coordinates. These mismatches make observation-specific appearances and sampling coordinates easier to reconstruct than stable signal structures, inducing observational shortcuts. We identify this failure mode as observation-biased pretraining.
items.author: Wenjin Gui, Junyu Shen, Haibo Xu et al.

items.title: Generalized Inverse Kinematics via Conditional Flow
items.summary: Inverse kinematics (IK) is a foundational primitive in robotics, mapping the task-space objectives expressed by higher-level planners to robot configurations that realize them. Traditional IK methods generally treat each query as an isolated pose-to-configuration problem, but planners often need a distribution over valid realizations that accounts for future reachability and preferences such as collision avoidance and stability. We introduce GenGenIK, a generative modeling approach that supports mobile bases, multiple end-effectors and targets, scene awareness, and preferences over robot behavior within a common interface. Experiments show that GenGenIK outperforms existing methods in both solve rate and runtime across tasks such as bimanual lift and flip-up, while allowing flexible control over the sampled distribution and remaining effective under partial scene observations.
items.author: Kaitlyn Zhang, Tomás Lozano-Pérez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling

items.title: What Conformal Selection Can Certify in CRISPR Off-Target Design:Benchmark Leakage, Free Baselines, and a Finite-Sample Cohort Requirement
items.summary: Conformal selection promises distribution-free, finite-sample control of the error rate of a decision, and has been proposed as a safety layer for machine-learning CRISPR guide design. We ask whether such a certificate is attainable from the validated off-target data that exist. The constraint is arithmetic: a conformal p-value cannot fall below one divided by the calibration cohort size plus one, so a Benjamini-Hochberg selection certifies a single candidate only when that cohort is at least the candidate pool size divided by the tolerated error rate. Public cohorts supply ten validated guides, whereas a pool of two thousand at a ten percent error rate needs twenty thousand; the accepted set is consequently empty in over ninety-six percent of splits.
items.author: Mohammad Malekpouri, Somayeh Lotfi

items.title: Testing Conversation Preservation Across LLM APIs: A Rule-Based Oracle for Detecting Silent Information Loss
items.summary: LLM applications increasingly rely on translators and compatibility layers to move conversations across APIs. Yet a translated request can be accepted by the target API while silently losing information about instruction roles, tool interactions, error states, or generation controls. We introduce isloss, a deterministic oracle for testing conversation-information preservation across LLM API translations. It maps source and translated requests and replies to a shared intermediate representation, ConvIR, and applies explicit rules to distinguish legitimate representation changes from information loss. Unlike schema validation or reference-based differential testing, isloss requires neither a reference translation nor additional model calls. It also distinguishes avoidable loss from degradation caused by target API limitations.
items.author: Xin Liu, Xu Han, Yuxin Wang et al.

items.title: Faithful in Steps: Improving Generalization and Citation in RAG via Query Decomposition
items.summary: Retrieval-augment generation is a prevalent strategy to mitigate hallucinations of LLMs. The attributable RAG (RAGQ) generates quotes for its answers. The quotes indicate which input contexts support the RAG to derive the answers, enhancing the answer's verifiability and trustworthiness. However, existing RAGQs exhibit significant degradation when dealing with questions that require multi-hop reasoning and multi-modal understanding, suffering from over-citation, implicit entity identification failure, and poor generalization. In this paper, we propose a novel RAGQ framework, namely QDRAG. QDRAG breaks down the input question into atomic subquestions to identify the implicit entities. Then, the reranker prunes context distractors to eliminate the downstream over-citation.
items.author: Yue Liu, Zhongying Ru, Shimin Di et al.

items.title: Analysis choices decide whether untrained networks beat trained ones at V1: a multiverse analysis of model-brain RSA
items.summary: Untrained convolutional networks have been reported to rival trained networks as models of visual cortex, and we had reported an untrained-network advantage over backpropagation at V1 in THINGS fMRI, together with a dependence on evaluation resolution. Under a pre-specified ridge readout, the untrained network scored below the trained one at every pooling grid (median r difference -0.043 at g = 4, 0 of 5 seeds positive), and also in MSE skill and per-fold r. In exploratory analyses, across 36 combinations of unit normalisation, distance measure and voxel normalisation (28 distinct analyses), the sign of the V1 contrast depended on the analysis (intervals above 0 in 5 and below 0 in 9 distinct analyses), and in our networks the resolution dependence of the original convention appeared in only one cell.
items.author: Nils Leutenegger

items.title: MAGIC: Modality-Aware Gini Inspection for Clinical Hallucination Detection in LMMs
items.summary: Recent advances in medical large multimodal models (LMMs) have brought promising progress to clinical decision support, yet hallucination, the generation of confident but clinically unverifiable outputs, poses a critical threat to the reliability demanded in high-stakes medical settings. Existing hallucination detection methods, predominantly designed for unimodal settings, fail to capture the visual-linguistic dynamics inherent to medical imaging. We formulate the problem of hallucination detection in LMMs as disproportionate distribution of attention weights across the modalities during answer token generation. We quantify modality-specific attention concentration across layers and heads using the Gini coefficient and demonstrate statistically significant redistribution of attention mass between visual and textual tokens in hallucinated responses.
items.author: Sachin Acharya, Niyoj Oli, Shishir Adhikari et al.

items.title: One Hierarchy, Many Sports: Hierarchy-Aligned Multi-Task Learning for Next-Shot Prediction
items.summary: Next-shot prediction in racket sports requires learning from event data with different match structures, recorded attributes, and label vocabularies. Table tennis, badminton, and tennis nevertheless share a hierarchy in which shots form rallies and rallies form higher scoring units. We present MT-HTA, a hierarchy-aligned multi-task Transformer that uses this structure to jointly predict the attributes of the next shot. A temporal Transformer captures event progression, a feature-token path models interactions among semantic fields rather than along the time axis, and task-specific attention retrieves information from hierarchical summaries and player context. The architecture supports three- and four-level hierarchies and sport-dependent task sets.
items.author: Chao-Wei Cai, Min-Te Sun, Sheng Kuang Wu et al.

items.title: Reading the Table: Sim-to-Real Game State Detection for the Chef's Hat Card Game
items.summary: Tabletop games offer a compelling scenario to study the interaction between artificial and human agents, combining social interaction with game state tracking and physical manipulation. To assess the game state, a robot needs to precisely detect closely related game objects, such as different card designs, requiring dedicated training data that is costly to annotate in the real world. Instead, we develop a fully automated synthetic data collection pipeline, using re-projection of known 3D coordinates to generate labels automatically and domain randomization to bridge the reality gap. This approach is used to collect a dataset of 25413 samples to finetune an object detection and a segmentation model, which are combined to assign detected cards to game-relevant zones and infer the game state.
items.author: Connor Gäde, Matthias Kerzel, Hauke Bünning et al.

items.title: An Approach to Hinton's Mother-Child Proposal: Neural Networks Learning and Preserving Care in a Finite World
items.summary: Hinton proposed that artificial intelligence should be given "maternal instincts" and relate to us as a mother to her child. We argue that care must first be learned, with the network itself as the child. We construct this upbringing in a finite world and study whether care survives the mother's departure, new situations and further learning. The mechanism combines a vocabulary of harm, a learned measure of future acceptability and an execution veto. A finite role certificate supports transfer within a declared world family. When the hidden representation changes, an update is accepted only if a care readout recovers the required judgements with a prescribed margin and bounded weights.
items.author: Csaba Balogh

items.title: GHAgentCI: A Dataset of Coding-Agent Invocations in CI Workflow Histories
items.summary: Coding agents are increasingly integrated into GitHub Actions to review pull requests, triage issues and modify code. Identifying these integrations is challenging because agentic workflows often resemble ordinary CI files, with evidence appearing in action references, shell commands and workflow conventions. We present GHAgentCI, a dataset of 15K+ workflow histories from 6K+ of 196K+ mined GitHub repositories, comprising 159K+ revisions and 205K+ agent-evidence records linked to workflow triggers and declared execution constraints. Our open-source extractor, cai-miner, detects agent-related evidence using an extensible catalogue. Manual validation of 576 stratified records confirmed 96.1% of dedicated-action matches and 98.8% of GitHub Agentic Workflow matches, with lower rates for other evidence kinds.
items.author: Daniel Ogenrwot, Jorge Gonzalo Delgado Cervantes, Woojoong Kim et al.

items.title: DecArena: Evaluating Large-Scale Decentralized Multi-Agent Collaboration
items.summary: Emerging personal AI agents raise fundamental scalability and privacy concerns for centralized multi-agent systems (MASs), which rely on a global orchestrator with broad access to agents, resources, and communication. In decentralized environments, global visibility is unavailable. Agents need to proactively discover non-local resources (e.g. tools, skills), and collaborate with other agents to solve tasks. We study decentralized multi-agent collaboration under graph-constrained communication, a natural reflection of human structures. Each agent observes only its local state and can interact only with neighboring agents. We introduce a benchmark with synthetic scalable distributed tool calling with 100K+ tools. Our experiments reveal that recent LLM agents struggle to discover non-local relevant resources and collaborate in decentralized setting.
items.author: Jiali Cheng, Oleg Rokhlenko, Joo-Kyung Kim et al.

items.title: Incentive-Responsive Agents: A Principal-Agent Framework, Metric Suite, and Runtime Architecture for Long-Lived Personal AI Agents
items.summary: Personal AI agents now persist: they hold accounts, mailboxes, long-term memory, and open-ended task streams, yet the dominant way to improve them remains capability-side: prompt engineering, larger models, longer thinking, and retrieval. We argue that long-lived agents are missing an incentive layer. We formalize an incentive not as text in a prompt but as a runtime contract over the agent's operating point (model tier, test-time compute, memory budget, tool authority, task priority, verification, and compensation) that the agent's policy must causally consume. We develop a principal-agent model with hidden effort, a contractible operating point, and costly verification. We derive (i) a non-consumption invariance principle separating genuine incentives from prompt-level persuasion, (ii) a persistence-as-discount theorem making identity continuity a precondition for sustained effort, (iii) an incentive-capability exchange-rate frontier yielding a per-task routing rule, and (iv) a Goodhart bound for multi-channel verification, plus a three-channel decomposition of mechanism gains (allocation, verification, continuation).
items.author: Jipu Su

items.title: ReShap: Interpretable Reinforcement Learning for High-Dimensional Multi-Action Settings
items.summary: Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) plays a crucial role in tackling complex tasks, yet its reliance on deep neural networks makes the learned policies opaque. To enhance the trustworthiness of RL policies, existing work (e.g., the SILVER framework [Li et al., 2025]) has focused on Shapley-based interpretability, but is typically restricted to low-dimensional state spaces, binary-action settings, and a single class of linear surrogate. We propose ReShap, a policy-distillation framework that extends Shapley-based interpretability to high-dimensional, multi-action environments. ReShap extracts compact feature representations from raw image observations, performs SHAP-based feature attribution to characterize how each feature contributes to the policy's decisions, and distills the deep RL policy into an interpretable surrogate trained on the full set of (state, policy-action) pairs along the policy's visited distribution.
items.author: Yiyu Qian, Pengfei Guo, Liyuan Zhao

items.title: Virus-Like Particles Improve Gene Editing in Pigs and Chickens
items.summary: Pigs and chickens are vital livestock and key model organisms for agricultural, translational, and biomedical research. While tools like CRISPR/Cas9 have advanced functional genomics, delivering these systems efficiently has remained a significant hurdle. Researchers have now addressed this limitation by using virus-like particles as delivery vehicles for genome engineering tools. Testing across porcine and avian models, the team found that virus-like particle delivery successfully enabled high CRISPR/Cas9 editing rates and efficient Cre recombination. In pigs, this worked well across cells, organoids, and oocytes. In chickens, the approach proved effective in cell cultures, tracheal organ cultures, and in ovo environments. Additional tests with reporter and dCas9 variants further highlighted the platform's broad utility. These results demonstrate that virus-like particles provide an efficient, time-saving method for livestock gene editing across various experimental models, benefiting animal health, agricultural productivity, and One Health research.
items.author: Theresa M. Pauli, Theresa von Heyl, Beate Rieblinger et al.
items.original_title: Virus-like particles enable highly efficient gene editing across porcine and avian in vitro , ex vivo , and in ovo models
items.original_summary: by Theresa M. Pauli, Theresa von Heyl, Beate Rieblinger, Sabrina Teresa Schleibinger, Wei Liang, Antonia Schmauser, Mithuoshni Arullmoli, Paul Derrer, Anika Eckstein, Sirradu Jagana, Camila Gatti Corrêa, Krzysztof Flisikowski, Tatiana Flisikowska, Benjamin Schusser Pigs and chickens are not only the most important livestock species for global food production but also serve as key model organisms in various research disciplines. The pig is widely used in translational research due to its anatomical and physiological similarity to humans, providing valuable insights into immunology, metabolism, and disease mechanisms. In contrast, the chicken has become an essential model for studies related to poultry health, animal welfare, and developmental biology.
items.ai_title: Virus-Like Particles Improve Gene Editing in Pigs and Chickens
items.ai_summary: Pigs and chickens are vital livestock and key model organisms for agricultural, translational, and biomedical research. While tools like CRISPR/Cas9 have advanced functional genomics, delivering these systems efficiently has remained a significant hurdle. Researchers have now addressed this limitation by using virus-like particles as delivery vehicles for genome engineering tools. Testing across porcine and avian models, the team found that virus-like particle delivery successfully enabled high CRISPR/Cas9 editing rates and efficient Cre recombination. In pigs, this worked well across cells, organoids, and oocytes. In chickens, the approach proved effective in cell cultures, tracheal organ cultures, and in ovo environments. Additional tests with reporter and dCas9 variants further highlighted the platform's broad utility. These results demonstrate that virus-like particles provide an efficient, time-saving method for livestock gene editing across various experimental models, benefiting animal health, agricultural productivity, and One Health research.

items.title: Evolutionary Origins of Paired Appendages and Genetic Rewiring
items.summary: A recent study investigates the evolutionary origins of dorsoventral polarity in paired appendages, comparing them to symmetric median fins. Researchers found that the lmx1b gene is located in the dorsal paired fin mesenchyme but shifts to a posterior position in median fins, pointing to the genetic rewiring of an ancient toolkit.

items.title: Unlocking the Invasion Mechanisms of Cryptosporidium Parasites
items.summary: Cryptosporidium is a major cause of severe diarrheal illness in young children, establishing a unique niche inside intestinal cells. Researchers utilized molecular markers to observe how the parasite invades host cells with high spatial and temporal resolution. The study reveals that the parasite anchors itself through the sequential discharge of specialized secretory organelles before entering the host. Additionally, a single rhoptry structure persists past the initial discharge to function as a conduit for multiple waves of effector proteins. Eventually, the rhoptry membrane transforms into the feeder organelle that divides the host and parasite cytoplasm, offering a clearer picture of intracellular parasitism.
items.author: Allison Cohen, Tim Bergner, Amandine Guérin et al.
items.original_title: The single Cryptosporidium rhoptry sequentially drives invasion and host-parasite interface formation
items.original_summary: by Allison Cohen, Tim Bergner, Amandine Guérin, Maryse Lebrun, Michael Laue, Christian Klotz, Boris Striepen The apicomplexan parasite Cryptosporidium is a leading cause of diarrheal disease in young children. Within the intestinal epithelium, Cryptosporidium establishes a unique intracellular niche in the apical brush border of enterocytes. A structurally complex interface between host and parasite acts as a holdfast and enables protein and metabolite transport. How the parasite invades its host cell and builds the interface is poorly understood. Here, we reveal parasite invasion with high temporal and spatial resolution using rigorous molecular markers. We find that sequential discharge of specialized secretory organelles anchors the parasite within the host prior to internalization.

items.title: Pepti-DrugPhAI: A Multimodal AI Tool for Peptide Drug Design
items.summary: Peptide drugs are promising therapeutics due to their high selectivity and activity, but poor pharmacokinetics often stall their development. To solve this, researchers developed Pepti-DrugPhAI, a multimodal algorithm capable of predicting the pharmacokinetics and toxicity of diverse peptide compounds. By simultaneously analyzing chemical structure SMILES representations and amino acid sequences, the algorithm efficiently handles canonical peptides, cyclic structures, and non-canonical modifications. The model evaluates critical ADMET parameters, membrane permeability, and toxicity profiles while calculating an adaptive suitability score based on biological activity. Tested against independent datasets, the tool demonstrates high accuracy and provides a valuable asset for selecting viable peptide drug candidates.
items.author: Elizaveta A. Bogdanova, Timofei F. Lukianov, Artem V. Chernukhin et al.
items.original_title: Pepti-DrugPhAI: Multimodal AI-evaluator for functional pharmacokinetics and toxicity of peptides
items.original_summary: by Elizaveta A. Bogdanova, Timofei F. Lukianov, Artem V. Chernukhin, Alexey K. Shaytan Peptide drugs exhibit exceptional selectivity for biological targets and high functional activity making them among the most promising therapeutic agents. However, unsatisfactory pharmacokinetic characteristics remain a critical barrier to their implementation. They often become the primary reason for the failure of promising candidates in preclinical and clinical trials. To address this issue, we present Pepti-DrugPhAI – a comprehensive algorithm for the precise prediction of the pharmacokinetics and toxicity of a wide range of peptide compounds. Unlike many existing solutions, the proposed algorithm is multimodal and can simultaneously process both SMILES representations of chemical structures and amino acid sequences.

items.title: Sphinx R Package Enhances Spatial Proteomics Analysis
items.summary: Spatial omics is vital for examining tissue microenvironmental heterogeneity, yet existing tools heavily favor transcriptomics over proteomics data. To bridge this gap, researchers introduced Sphinx, an R package designed to offer a complete spatial proteomics workflow encompassing preprocessing, cell annotation, spatial neighborhood modeling, and functional characterization. Sphinx introduces an adaptive parameter selection framework driven by spatial statistical metrics, alongside computational optimizations tailored for large-scale datasets. The software efficiently identifies distinct cell types and spatial functional units, such as tertiary lymphoid structures, across various tissue datasets including lung adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, and mouse spleen. By improving scalability and computational performance, Sphinx enables deeper characterization of tissue microenvironments and spatial organization.
items.author: Mengyi Yan, Xiaoxiu Tan, Zhenhao Liu et al.
items.original_title: Sphinx: An R package for adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling and functional analysis in spatial omics
items.original_summary: by Mengyi Yan, Xiaoxiu Tan, Zhenhao Liu, Siwen Zhang, Yiwen Du, Hong Li, Lanming Chen, Lu Xie Spatial omics enables analysis of tissue microenvironmental heterogeneity, but most spatial tools are optimized for transcriptomics and poorly suited to proteomics data. We developed Sphinx, an R package providing a comprehensive workflow for spatial proteomics, including preprocessing, cell annotation, adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling, and functional characterization. Importantly, it introduces an adaptive parameter selection framework guided by spatial statistical metrics and incorporates computational optimizations for large-scale datasets, enabling robust neighborhood modeling. Notably, Sphinx offers improved computational efficiency and scalability. Across lung adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, and mouse spleen datasets, Sphinx robustly identifies cell types and spatial functional units, including tertiary lymphoid structures.

items.title: Investigating Burst-to-Burst Neural Coordination and Rhythm Resetting
items.summary: Networks of bursting neurons drive robust sequential rhythms in multiple neural systems, such as central pattern generators that oversee motor activity. A recent study combines biophysical models of the pyloric central pattern generator with electrophysiological experiments to examine cycle-by-cycle coordination resetting. Researchers analyzed variability constraints of sequence intervals determined by burst onset and offset timing references. The study successfully identified the conditions that prompt sequential dynamical invariants to emerge as robust relationships within a cycle, as well as when these relations reset or span across consecutive cycles during slow modulatory actions.
items.author: Pablo Sanchez-Martin, Irene Elices, Alicia Garrido-Peña et al.
items.original_title: Burst-to-burst information resetting in sequential rhythmic neural activity
items.original_summary: by Pablo Sanchez-Martin, Irene Elices, Alicia Garrido-Peña, Carlos Garcia-Saura, Rafael Levi, Francisco B. Rodriguez, Pablo Varona In multiple neural systems, networks of bursting neurons generate and coordinate robust sequential rhythms, such as those observed in central pattern generators (CPGs) that control motor activity. In this paper, we combine electrophysiological experiments and biophysical models of the pyloric CPG to investigate cycle-by-cycle coordination resetting in sequential rhythms. In particular, we focus our analysis on the variability constraints of sequence intervals defined by the burst onset and offset time references, which structure the timing of the rhythmic CPG sequence cycle-by-cycle. We identified the conditions under which sequential dynamical invariants emerge as robust relationships between specific intervals within the same cycle, and when such relations reset at each cycle or extend between intervals of consecutive cycles.

items.title: Protein Language Model Improves Antibody Binding Affinity
items.summary: Researchers have introduced Ab-Affinity, a fine-tuned protein language model designed to predict antibody binding affinity against target peptides in the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. When combined with a genetic algorithm and simulated annealing for sequence optimization, Ab-Affinity successfully generated candidate antibodies with over a 100-fold increase in predicted binding affinity compared to their natural parental counterparts. Molecular docking and dynamics simulations indicated that these synthetic candidates have enhanced stability and interactions with the target peptide epitope. Additionally, in vitro experimental testing on a top candidate showed increased binding relative to the original antibody. The developers have publicly released all analysis pipelines, source code, and model weights to support reproducibility.

items.original_summary: by Faisal Bin Ashraf, Karen Paco, Sanaz Zebardast, Zihao Zhang, Ryan Mooney, Christian J. Dávila Ojeda, Mariana Paco Mendivil, Rashid M. Alam, Eva Chen, Iraneus Ogu, Jordan A. Here we introduce Ab-Affinity, a fine-tuned protein language model (PLM) that predicts the binding affinity of an antibody against a target peptide within the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.

items.title: New Framework Decodes Transcriptional Bursting from Single-Cell Data
items.summary: Scientists have developed PhysInfer, an unsupervised framework that uses a physics-constrained neural network to infer transcriptional burst dynamics from static single-cell RNA sequencing data. The method addresses parameter unidentifiability and model mismatch by employing a physics-informed loss function that combines stationary-distribution likelihood with zero-count anchoring. This transforms microscopic rates into interpretable macroscopic burst-quantity representations of frequency and size. Validated on synthetic datasets, PhysInfer accurately recovers parameters in low-to-medium activation regimes. Applied to mouse embryonic fibroblast data, the tool successfully mapped a transcriptional dynamic manifold across thousands of genes, and its adaptive topology module identified specific genes supporting a sequential three-state representation, offering an improved approach for characterizing gene expression patterns.
items.author: Xiaodong Zeng, Jingwen Zhang, Shan Li et al.
items.original_title: PhysInfer: A physics-constrained neural network for adaptive inference of transcriptional bursting from single-cell RNA-seq
items.original_summary: by Xiaodong Zeng, Jingwen Zhang, Shan Li, Haohua Wang Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has established that gene expression is driven by stochastic transcriptional bursting. However, inferring burst dynamics from static scRNA-seq snapshots is fundamentally constrained by parameter unidentifiability and model topology mismatch. Here, we propose PhysInfer, an unsupervised framework that integrates a physics-constrained neural network with adaptive model selection and parameter decoupling. A physics-informed loss function, combining stationary-distribution likelihood with zero-count anchoring, reparameterizes the optimization from unidentifiable microscopic rates to an interpretable macroscopic burst-quantity representation of burst size and burst frequency, thereby providing an interpretable parameterization for assessing practical recoverability in static data.

items.title: Method Uses Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem to Detect Brain Memory Effects
items.summary: A central question in neuroscience is how the brain balances local and distributed information processing across different conscious states. Researchers suggest this balance relies on memory effects, where a region's future activity depends on past feedback from the wider network. To study this, the team introduced the FDTest, a technique that evaluates local memory effects by measuring violations of a generalized Fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Testing whole-brain models fitted to human neuroimaging data showed that memory structure aligns with underlying brain connectivity. Furthermore, when applied to individuals during wakefulness and deep sleep, the method revealed stronger memory effects during wakefulness, highlighting more integrated dynamics. The findings suggest local memory is a reliable dynamical marker for different brain states.
items.author: Sebastian Manuel Geli, Juan Manuel Monti, Adrián Ponce-Alvarez et al.
items.original_title: FDTest: Fluctuation-dissipation theorem as a test for memory effects in brain dynamics
items.original_summary: by Sebastian Manuel Geli, Juan Manuel Monti, Adrián Ponce-Alvarez, Gustavo Deco, Yonatan Sanz Perl A central challenge in neuroscience is to understand how the brain flexibly balances local and distributed information processing to support diverse cognitive and conscious states. We hypothesize that a key signature of this balance is the presence of memory effects, which arise when a brain region’s future activity depends not only on its current state, but also on past information fed back from the wider network. Here we introduce the FDTest, a method for assessing local memory effects in multidimensional systems by measuring violations of a generalized Fluctuation–dissipation theorem (FDT).

items.title: Tachykinin-like Signaling Modulates Thermotaxis in Caenorhabditis elegans
items.summary: Mammalian Neurokinin B signaling is linked to menopausal thermoregulatory issues, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. To study this, researchers utilized Caenorhabditis elegans thermotaxis as a model system for conserved tachykinin signaling. They found that overexpressing nlp-58, the nematode ortholog of mammalian NKB, leads to abnormal thermotaxis behaviors without altering thermosensory neuron temperature responses. This defect is mediated primarily via the tachykinin receptor TKR-1 in specific sensory neurons, and can be partially alleviated by treatment with fezolinetant, a clinical NK3R antagonist used for menopausal symptoms. The findings establish an NLP-58 and TKR-1 signaling pathway that modulates thermotaxis and provides a model for studying conserved circuit modulation.
items.author: Moon Sun Jang, Hironori J. Matsuyama, Ryoga Suzuki et al.
items.original_title: Tachykinin-like NLP-58 signaling through TKR-1 modulates thermotaxis behavior in Caenorhabditis elegans
items.original_summary: by Moon Sun Jang, Hironori J. Matsuyama, Ryoga Suzuki, King Chuen Law, Yukimasa Shibata, Xiaolin Zhang, Koutarou D. Kimura, Yukihiko Kubota, Masahiro Ito, Kiyoji Nishiwaki, Ikue Mori Neurokinin B (NKB) signaling plays a central role in mammalian thermoregulatory dysfunction associated with menopause, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we establish Caenorhabditis elegans thermotaxis as a genetically tractable system for investigating conserved tachykinin signaling. We demonstrate that overexpression of nlp-58 , the C. elegans ortholog of mammalian NKB, induces abnormal thermotaxis behavior without impairing the temperature response of the thermosensory neurons. NLP-58 is expressed in multiple neurons, including the AIY interneurons, a central integrative node of the thermosensory circuit.

items.title: Baloxavir and Molnupiravir Protect Immunosuppressed Hamsters from H5N1 Infection
items.summary: Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) poses ongoing zoonotic risks, and immunosuppressed individuals often face severe disease with limited antiviral guidance. Researchers evaluated the pathogenesis of an H5N1 human isolate in cyclophosphamide-immunosuppressed hamsters and tested several antiviral treatments. While normal hamsters cleared the virus, immunosuppressed subjects suffered 75% mortality, prolonged viral replication, and neuroinvasion. In treatment trials, baloxavir achieved 100% survival, shortened viral shedding, reduced inflammation, and prevented neuroinvasion. High-dose molnupiravir and certain combination therapies also prevented mortality and cleared the virus from lung and brain tissues. In contrast, oseltamivir and low-dose molnupiravir showed limited effectiveness against severe clinical signs. These results highlight baloxavir and molnupiravir regimens as promising therapeutic strategies for severe H5N1 infections.
items.author: Andrea Arroyave, Henintsoa Rabezanahary, Ahmed Sahli et al.
items.original_title: Baloxavir and molnupiravir protect against severe influenza A(H5N1) infection in immunosuppressed hamsters
items.original_summary: by Andrea Arroyave, Henintsoa Rabezanahary, Ahmed Sahli, Mariana Baz Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) viruses continue to expand their geographic and host range, raising concerns about zoonotic transmission and pandemic preparedness. Immunocompromised individuals often develop severe and prolonged disease, yet evidence guiding antiviral therapy remains limited. Here, we characterized the pathogenesis and assessed direct-contact transmission of an influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b genotype D1.1 virus recently isolated from a human case in British Columbia, Canada, in cyclophosphamide-immunosuppressed hamsters, with normal hamsters included for comparison of infection outcomes and viral shedding kinetics. We also evaluated the antiviral efficacy of oseltamivir (20 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days), baloxavir (50 mg/kg, 2 doses), and molnupiravir (50 or 200 mg/kg twice daily) as monotherapies or in combination (oseltamivir with low-dose molnupiravir) in immunosuppressed hamsters.
